questions.explanation_zh: 第2句“without spending a cent”意为分文不花、完全免费。
distractor_reasons: 正确：nothing at all 对应 without spending a cent。
错误：无需押金。
错误：不按秋季销售额分成。
错误：未提邮费。

questions.stem: What are borrowers encouraged to submit along with returned seeds in autumn?
options: Notes describing drought resistance and flavor.
Soil samples sealed in glass bottles.
Receipt copies from gardening tool stores.
Photographs of garden pests for inspection.
questions.answer: Notes describing drought resistance and flavor.

evidence_anchor.text_span: After the autumn harvest, borrowers dry seeds from their healthiest plants and return a fresh batch alongside notes on drought tolerance and taste.

questions.key_evidence_line: After the autumn harvest, borrowers dry seeds from their healthiest plants and return a fresh batch alongside notes on drought tolerance and taste.
questions.explanation_zh: 第3句提到归还留种时需附上关于耐旱性（drought tolerance）和口感（taste）的记录。
distractor_reasons: 正确：drought resistance and flavor 同义替换 drought tolerance and taste。
错误：未提玻璃瓶装土样。
错误：未提工具店收据。
错误：未提害虫照片。

listening_cases.title: Ferry Terminal Roofs Become Pop-Up Repair Workshops on Sundays
listening_cases.title_zh: 新闻听力：轮渡码头屋顶变身周日流动修补集市

transcript_lines.speaker: Anchor
transcript_lines.text: Starting this month, a harbor transit terminal is opening its sheltered panoramic deck every Sunday afternoon as a neighborhood repair clinic.
transcript_lines.text_zh: 从本月起，一座海港交通枢纽站每周日下午开放其有顶棚的全景平台，用作社区修补诊所。

transcript_lines.speaker: Anchor
transcript_lines.text: Retired electricians, tailors, and bicycle mechanics volunteer at long folding tables, teaching residents how to fix toasted switches, torn backpacks, and squeaky brakes instead of tossing them away.
transcript_lines.text_zh: 退休电工、裁缝和自行车维修师志愿坐在长折叠桌前，教居民如何修理烤面包机开关、破损背包和异响刹车，而不是一丢了之。

transcript_lines.speaker: Anchor
transcript_lines.text: Visitors only pay if a brand-new replacement fuse or zipper must be ordered from a supplier.
transcript_lines.text_zh: 访客仅在需要向供应商订购全新保险丝或拉链备件时才需支付零件费。

transcript_lines.speaker: Anchor
transcript_lines.text: Organizers say teaching repair skills builds confidence among commuters waiting between island ferry departures while keeping nearly four tons of household items out of landfills.
transcript_lines.text_zh: 组织者表示，传授修理技能不仅能让等待海岛渡轮发船的乘客学到本领，还减少了近四吨家居物品进入垃圾填埋场。

questions.stem: When does the harbor terminal host its neighborhood repair clinic?
options: Every Friday morning during rush hour.
On the last Saturday night of each quarter.
Daily whenever ferry sailings are canceled.
questions.answer: Every Sunday afternoon.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Starting this month, a harbor transit terminal is opening its sheltered panoramic deck every Sunday afternoon as a neighborhood repair clinic.

questions.key_evidence_line: Starting this month, a harbor transit terminal is opening its sheltered panoramic deck every Sunday afternoon as a neighborhood repair clinic.
questions.explanation_zh: 首句指出每周日下午（every Sunday afternoon）开放。
distractor_reasons: 正确：与首句时间一致。
错误：非周五早高峰。
错误：非每季度最后一个周六夜晚。
错误：定期在周日举办，而非仅在停航时。

questions.stem: How do the volunteers assist residents who bring broken belongings?
options: They guide residents in fixing appliances, bags, and bicycles themselves.
They ship damaged electronics back to original factories.
They trade broken items for unused lost-and-found luggage.
They buy old bicycles to rebuild ferry station racks.
questions.answer: They guide residents in fixing appliances, bags, and bicycles themselves.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Retired electricians, tailors, and bicycle mechanics volunteer at long folding tables, teaching residents how to fix toasted switches, torn backpacks, and squeaky brakes instead of tossing them away.

questions.key_evidence_line: Retired electricians, tailors, and bicycle mechanics volunteer at long folding tables, teaching residents how to fix toasted switches, torn backpacks, and squeaky brakes instead of tossing them away.
questions.explanation_zh: 第2句重点是志愿者教居民动手修（teaching residents how to fix...），传递可持续维修技能。
distractor_reasons: 正确：紧扣 teaching residents how to fix。
错误：并非寄回原厂维修。
错误：未提失物招领箱包置换。
错误：未提收购旧自行车。

questions.stem: What environmental impact has the repair clinic already achieved?
options: It kept almost four tons of household items away from landfills.
It cut harbor ferry fuel use by replacing diesel engines.
It eliminated paper boarding passes on weekend routes.
It planted rooftop herb gardens along both seawalls.
questions.answer: It kept almost four tons of household items away from landfills.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Organizers say teaching repair skills builds confidence among commuters waiting between island ferry departures while keeping nearly four tons of household items out of landfills.

questions.key_evidence_line: Organizers say teaching repair skills builds confidence among commuters waiting between island ferry departures while keeping nearly four tons of household items out of landfills.
questions.explanation_zh: 末句提到项目使近四吨家居物品免于进入垃圾填埋场。
distractor_reasons: 正确：almost four tons ... away from landfills 对应 nearly four tons ... out of landfills。

listening_cases.title: Evaluating Peer Micro-Tutoring Pairs in Freshman Calculus

transcript_lines.text: Surprisingly yes, especially because we stopped pairing top scorers directly with the lowest scorers and grouped students just one step apart instead.

transcript_lines.speaker: Maya

reading_passages.title: Campus Bike-Sharing Needs More Than Parked Bicycles
reading_passages.title_zh: 校园共享单车不仅需要投放车辆

paragraphs.text: When several universities introduced brightly painted shared bicycles five years ago, administrators assumed that placing hundreds of bikes outside dormitories would instantly solve morning traffic congestion. During the first month, students enthusiastically adopted the green commute, praising the speed between distant lecture halls and enjoying the fresh air before early seminars. By mid-semester, however, broken chains, flat tires, and uneven parking left popular gates cluttered while outlying labs had almost no bikes available.

Researchers studying campus mobility point out that hardware alone never creates a sustainable transport system. Without scheduled maintenance crews and smart redistribution vans, shared fleets quickly lose reliability across sprawling campuses. When riders repeatedly encounter damaged brakes or empty racks right before a morning quiz, they abandon cycling and crowd back onto campus shuttle buses, worsening the very delays the program meant to reduce.

To reverse this pattern, Greenfield College decided to implement a digital incentive scheme last autumn. Instead of penalizing every late parking mistake with heavy fines, the student transport office rewarded riders who returned bikes to designated uphill racks where demand was highest. Even small credits redeemable for library printing or campus coffee shifted daily parking habits within three weeks. Formerly empty hilltop stations soon became reliable pickup points for morning classes.

Equally important, the college published a weekly repair map showing which docks had been inspected and inviting students to flag loose pedals in ten seconds. Because maintenance teams responded within two hours, trust in the fleet recovered steadily throughout the spring term. Campus planners now emphasize that lasting green habits depend less on buying extra bicycles than on consistent upkeep, clear parking rules, and practical user feedback. Several neighboring colleges have already copied the model.

questions.stem: What problem appeared by mid-semester after universities first introduced shared bicycles?
options: Damaged bikes and uneven distribution left some areas cluttered and others empty.
Shuttle bus drivers went on strike because fewer students rode buses.
Students refused to ride bicycles from the very first day of the program.
Local police banned brightly painted bicycles from public roads.
questions.answer: Damaged bikes and uneven distribution left some areas cluttered and others empty.
questions.evidence_text: By mid-semester, however, broken chains, flat tires, and uneven parking left popular gates cluttered while outlying labs had almost no bikes available.

evidence_anchor.text_span: By mid-semester, however, broken chains, flat tires, and uneven parking left popular gates cluttered while outlying labs had almost no bikes available.

questions.explanation_zh: 定位第1段转折词 however 后的句子：broken chains, flat tires（损坏车辆）与 uneven parking left popular gates cluttered while outlying labs had almost no bikes（分布不均）。
distractor_reasons: 正确：直接对应第1段末句关于车辆损坏与停放分布不均的描述。
错误：第2段提到学生重新挤上校车，并未提到校车司机罢工（无中生有）。
错误：第1段第2句说首月学生热情很高（enthusiastically adopted），与“从第一天起拒绝”矛盾。
错误：文章未提及警方禁止共享单车。

questions.stem: According to Paragraph 2, why do students return to riding campus shuttle buses?
options: Repeated failures to find working bikes make cycling unreliable.
Shuttle buses offer free coffee credits to morning riders.
Cycling between distant lecture halls takes longer than walking.
Repair crews forbid students from using bikes before quizzes.

questions.evidence_text: When riders repeatedly encounter damaged brakes or empty racks right before a morning quiz, they abandon cycling and crowd back onto campus shuttle buses, worsening the very delays the program meant to reduce.

questions.explanation_zh: 第2段指出当骑行者在早间小测前屡次遇到刹车损坏或空车架时，就会放弃骑车并重新挤上校车；题干选项将 damaged brakes or empty racks 同义改写为 failures to find working bikes。
distractor_reasons: 正确：同义概括了第2段中车况受损与无车可用的情况导致骑行失去可靠性。
错误：咖啡积分是第3段还车奖励政策，属于“张冠李戴”。
错误：第1段曾赞赏教学楼间骑行速度很快，与“比走路慢”相悖。
错误：文中未说维修队禁止学生使用单车。

questions.stem: How did Greenfield College encourage students to park bikes at uphill racks?
options: By offering small credits usable for printing or campus coffee.
By imposing heavy financial fines on every student.
By closing all downhill parking zones permanently.
By giving extra course grades to transport volunteers.
questions.answer: By offering small credits usable for printing or campus coffee.
questions.evidence_text: Even small credits redeemable for library printing or campus coffee shifted daily parking habits within three weeks.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Even small credits redeemable for library printing or campus coffee shifted daily parking habits within three weeks.

questions.explanation_zh: 定位第3段：学校采用激励而非重罚（Instead of penalizing... with heavy fines），提供可兑换图书馆打印或校园咖啡的小额积分（small credits）。
distractor_reasons: 正确：第3段末句明确提及可兑换打印或咖啡的积分改变了停放习惯。

questions.stem: What is the main message of the final paragraph?
options: Steady maintenance and responsive feedback matter more than simply adding bikes.
Buying double the number of bicycles will eliminate all repair delays.
Students prefer reporting broken pedals over riding uphill.
Campus planners plan to replace shared bikes with electric buses.
questions.answer: Steady maintenance and responsive feedback matter more than simply adding bikes.
questions.evidence_text: Campus planners now emphasize that lasting green habits depend less on buying extra bicycles than on consistent upkeep, clear parking rules, and practical user feedback.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Campus planners now emphasize that lasting green habits depend less on buying extra bicycles than on consistent upkeep, clear parking rules, and practical user feedback.

questions.explanation_zh: 第4段末句通过 depend less on A than on B 结构总结主旨：持久的绿色出行习惯与其靠多买车，不如靠持续维护（consistent upkeep）、清晰规则与用户反馈。
distractor_reasons: 正确：准确概括第4段末句“维护与反馈比盲目增车更重要”的核心结论。
错误：原文强调 depend less on buying extra bicycles，此项与结论相反。
错误：脱离主旨且曲解“10秒报修”机制的含义。
错误：文中未提及改用电动公交替代单车。

reading_passages.title: Reclaiming Deep Reading in an Age of Quick Alerts
reading_passages.title_zh: 在即时提醒时代重拾深度阅读

paragraphs.text: College instructors across disciplines report a striking decline in how long students can stay with a dense academic passage without checking a screen. Although young adults read thousands of short messages daily, rapid skimming trains the mind to hunt for isolated headlines rather than trace an argument across several paragraphs. When assigned a complex essay, many learners lose track of subtle transitions, evidence, and key counterarguments before reaching the third page.

Cognitive psychologists note that every phone alert creates a quiet cost even when a reader does not unlock the device. Resisting a vibration consumes mental energy, leaving less capacity for reading comprehension and logical comparison. As a result, students who keep social apps silent on the desk often finish a chapter faster and retain far more supporting detail during evening review sessions and seminar discussions.

Yet eliminating digital distraction does not require throwing away smartphones or retreating to isolated cabins. In a recent campus trial, two hundred sophomores practiced a simple twenty-minute routine: placing phones inside a zippered backpack, setting a gentle timer, and writing one sentence in the margin after every two paragraphs. Within a month, participants showed noticeable gains on unfamiliar inference questions, while reporting far less frustration with dense scholarly articles and lab manuals.

The researchers caution against treating deep reading as an all-or-nothing marathon that demands hours of unbroken silence every evening. Short, consistent sessions build mental stamina much like interval running strengthens the heart. Once learners experience the satisfaction of following a complex idea from premise to conclusion without interruption, resisting quick alerts feels less like a sacrifice and more like a relief. Good habits start small and grow steadily when practiced without unnecessary pressure.

questions.stem: According to Paragraph 1, how does reading many short messages daily affect students?
options: It trains them to look for isolated headlines rather than follow longer arguments.
It doubles the speed at which they summarize multi-paragraph essays.
It prevents them from understanding any words on a digital screen.
It motivates them to read printed academic books every evening.
questions.answer: It trains them to look for isolated headlines rather than follow longer arguments.
questions.evidence_text: Although young adults read thousands of short messages daily, rapid skimming trains the mind to hunt for isolated headlines rather than trace an argument across several paragraphs.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Although young adults read thousands of short messages daily, rapid skimming trains the mind to hunt for isolated headlines rather than trace an argument across several paragraphs.

questions.explanation_zh: 第1段指出虽然学生每天看上千条短消息，但快速浏览（rapid skimming）训练大脑去抓取孤立标题，而不是跨段落追踪完整论证。
distractor_reasons: 正确：直接对应第1段末句 hunt for isolated headlines rather than trace an argument。
错误：第1段并未说提高长文总结速度，反而指出难以追踪多段论证。
错误：“完全无法理解屏幕上的任何词”属于极端绝对化错项。
错误：本段开头提到学生持续阅读学术文章的时间正在下降（decline），并非激励多读纸质书。

questions.stem: Why does an ignored phone vibration still harm reading comprehension?
options: Holding back the urge to check it still uses up mental energy.
Phone vibrations physically damage printed paper on the desk.
Students forget how to unlock their devices after twenty minutes.
Social apps automatically delete saved reading notes.
questions.answer: Holding back the urge to check it still uses up mental energy.
questions.evidence_text: Resisting a vibration consumes mental energy, leaving less capacity for reading comprehension and logical comparison.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Resisting a vibration consumes mental energy, leaving less capacity for reading comprehension and logical comparison.

questions.explanation_zh: 第2段解释了“即使不解锁手机也有隐性代价”：克制查看振动的冲动会消耗精力（Resisting a vibration consumes mental energy），从而压缩理解与逻辑比较的容量。
distractor_reasons: 正确：准确同义转述 Resisting a vibration consumes mental energy。
错误：文中讨论认知精力消耗，而非物理损坏纸张。
错误：无中生有。
错误：无中生有。

questions.stem: What did sophomores do in the twenty-minute campus trial described in Paragraph 3?
options: Put phones out of sight in a backpack and wrote brief margin summaries.
Abandoned smartphones completely for an entire academic semester.
Moved to quiet mountain cabins to memorize dictionary lists.
Read aloud in pairs without setting any timer.
questions.answer: Put phones out of sight in a backpack and wrote brief margin summaries.
questions.evidence_text: In a recent campus trial, two hundred sophomores practiced a simple twenty-minute routine: placing phones inside a zippered backpack, setting a gentle timer, and writing one sentence in the margin after every two paragraphs.

evidence_anchor.text_span: In a recent campus trial, two hundred sophomores practiced a simple twenty-minute routine: placing phones inside a zippered backpack, setting a gentle timer, and writing one sentence in the margin after every two paragraphs.

questions.explanation_zh: 第3段详述了校园实验的三步做法：把手机放进拉链背包、设温和计时器、每读两段在页边写一句话总结。
distractor_reasons: 正确：概括了“把手机装进背包 + 页边写一句话总结”的实验做法。
错误：第3段首句明确说不需要扔掉手机（does not require throwing away smartphones），此项夸大。
错误：第3段首句否定“退隐孤立木屋（retreating to isolated cabins）”，属于反义混淆。
错误：实验要求设计时器且独立阅读写批注，并非双人朗读。

questions.stem: Why does the author compare short, consistent reading sessions to "interval running" in Paragraph 4?
options: To show that regular brief practice steadily builds reading endurance.
To suggest that students should read while jogging outdoors.
To prove that physical exercise replaces academic study.
To argue that marathon reading is the only way to pass exams.
questions.answer: To show that regular brief practice steadily builds reading endurance.
questions.evidence_text: Short, consistent sessions build mental stamina much like interval running strengthens the heart.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Short, consistent sessions build mental stamina much like interval running strengthens the heart.

questions.explanation_zh: 第4段用间歇跑增强心肺功能作比喻，说明短而持续的阅读训练（Short, consistent sessions）能够建立心智耐力（mental stamina）。
distractor_reasons: 正确：准确解释了类比“间歇跑”的修辞目的——短时规律训练培养耐力。
错误：把类比当成了字面建议（一边跑步一边阅读），属于望文生义。
错误：文中并未说体育锻炼可以替代学业。
错误：第4段首句明确反对把深度阅读当成“要么全做要么不做”的马拉松（caution against treating... as an all-or-nothing marathon）。

questions.stem: How do learners feel once they experience uninterrupted deep reading, according to the end of the passage?
options: Avoiding quick alerts feels like a welcome relief rather than a loss.
They miss checking messages every two minutes.
They feel exhausted from writing margin notes.
They decide to delete all educational apps permanently.
questions.answer: Avoiding quick alerts feels like a welcome relief rather than a loss.
questions.evidence_text: Once learners experience the satisfaction of following a complex idea from premise to conclusion without interruption, resisting quick alerts feels less like a sacrifice and more like a relief.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Once learners experience the satisfaction of following a complex idea from premise to conclusion without interruption, resisting quick alerts feels less like a sacrifice and more like a relief.

questions.explanation_zh: 定位文章最后一句：less like a sacrifice and more like a relief（与其说是牺牲，不如说是一种解脱），说明学习者感受到的是轻松与解脱。
distractor_reasons: 正确：直接对应 less like a sacrifice and more like a relief。
错误：与“获得专注的满足感”相反。
错误：文中强调的是满足感（satisfaction）和解脱感（relief），未说写批注令人精疲力竭。
错误：原文未提及永久删除所有教育类应用。

reading_passages.title: Vertical Farms Inside Repurposed City Buildings
reading_passages.title_zh: 改造城市建筑中的垂直农场

paragraphs.text: Walk past an old brick warehouse near the eastern harbor, and you might expect dusty storage crates inside. Instead, engineers have transformed the building into an innovative vertical farm where rows of lettuce, herbs, and strawberries grow on stacked shelves under tuned pink light. By placing production inside the city, groceries receive fresh harvests within hours rather than days. That proximity sharply reduces spoilage during long highway transit and keeps delicate produce crisp for busy shoppers.

Unlike conventional open fields that lose moisture through evaporation and runoff, closed indoor racks recycle misted nutrients continuously. As a result, these facilities consume up to ninety percent less water per kilogram of greens while avoiding chemical sprays altogether. Controlled indoor temperatures also protect fragile crops from sudden frosts or summer heatwaves, enabling a reliable year-round yield regardless of local climate swings and seasonal droughts.

Still, vertical farming faces sharp economic limits that supporters must acknowledge honestly before building new sites across dense neighborhoods. Because artificial lighting and climate sensors require heavy electricity, running stacked farms is far more expensive than cultivating grains under free sunlight. For now, indoor farms make financial sense mainly for fast-growing, high-value leafy greens rather than staple crops like wheat or rice that demand vast acreage and cheap energy.

To improve energy efficiency, newer urban growers are pairing rooftop solar panels with waste heat captured from nearby data centers and commercial bakeries. Agricultural economists note that vertical farms will not replace rural farmland anytime soon; however, as a targeted partner to traditional harvests, they help cities conserve water, shorten supply chains, and keep nutritious produce accessible during extreme weather. Balanced planning keeps both food production models viable and resilient.

questions.stem: What advantage of placing vertical farms inside the city is mentioned in Paragraph 1?
options: Grocery stores can receive freshly harvested produce within hours.
Old brick warehouses require zero renovation before planting.
Outdoor sunlight reaches the bottom shelves automatically.
Crops grow without any electricity or lighting.
questions.answer: Grocery stores can receive freshly harvested produce within hours.
questions.evidence_text: By placing production inside the city, groceries receive fresh harvests within hours rather than days.

evidence_anchor.text_span: By placing production inside the city, groceries receive fresh harvests within hours rather than days.

questions.explanation_zh: 第1段末句明确指出：将生产放在城市内部后，杂货店/超市能在几小时内（而非几天后）收到新鲜采收的农产品。
distractor_reasons: 正确：直接对应第1段末句 groceries receive fresh harvests within hours。
错误：第1段说工程师对仓库进行了改造（transformed），并非零改造成本。
错误：第1段说明作物是在调好波段的粉光（tuned pink light）下生长，第3段也提到了人工照明。
错误：与第3段“人工照明与温控需要大量电力”直接矛盾。

questions.stem: How do closed indoor racks save water compared with open fields?
options: They continuously reuse misted nutrient water inside sealed loops.
They rely entirely on natural summer rainfall.
They grow only desert plants that need no moisture.
They freeze soil blocks to stop plant roots from absorbing water.
questions.answer: They continuously reuse misted nutrient water inside sealed loops.
questions.evidence_text: Unlike conventional open fields that lose moisture through evaporation and runoff, closed indoor racks recycle misted nutrients continuously.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Unlike conventional open fields that lose moisture through evaporation and runoff, closed indoor racks recycle misted nutrients continuously.

questions.explanation_zh: 第2段首句将封闭室内架与传统露天农田对比，指出其核心节水机制是持续循环利用雾化营养液（recycle misted nutrients continuously），选项用 reuse 同义替换 recycle。
distractor_reasons: 正确：reuse 准确同义替换原文第2段的 recycle。
错误：室内农场不靠露天降雨。
错误：第1段列举的是生菜、香草和草莓，并非沙漠植物。
错误：文中未提及冷冻土块。

questions.stem: Why are wheat and rice currently unsuitable for indoor vertical farms?
options: High electricity costs for lighting make staple grains unprofitable indoors.
Consumers refuse to eat grains harvested inside cities.
Indoor sensors cannot measure moisture in grain stalks.
Government rules ban growing wheat near harbor areas.
questions.answer: High electricity costs for lighting make staple grains unprofitable indoors.
questions.evidence_text: Because artificial lighting and climate sensors require heavy electricity, running stacked farms is far more expensive than cultivating grains under free sunlight.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Because artificial lighting and climate sensors require heavy electricity, running stacked farms is far more expensive than cultivating grains under free sunlight.

questions.explanation_zh: 第3段指出人工照明和气候传感器耗电量大（require heavy electricity），成本远高于免费阳光下种植谷物，因此目前只在经济上适合快生高价值的叶菜类。
distractor_reasons: 正确：从高电费成本推导出主粮在室内不划算（make financial sense mainly for... leafy greens rather than staple crops）。
错误：文中未提消费者抵制城市产谷物。
错误：文中未提传感器无法测量谷物水分。
错误：文中未提政府禁令。

questions.stem: What role do agricultural economists expect vertical farms to play in the near future?
options: A focused complement to traditional rural farming rather than a replacement.
A complete replacement for all countryside farms within five years.
A short-lived experiment limited to harbor museums.
A luxury project designed only for exporting strawberries.
questions.answer: A focused complement to traditional rural farming rather than a replacement.
questions.evidence_text: Agricultural economists note that vertical farms will not replace rural farmland anytime soon; however, as a targeted partner to traditional harvests, they help cities conserve water, shorten supply chains, and keep nutritious produce accessible during extreme weather.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Agricultural economists note that vertical farms will not replace rural farmland anytime soon; however, as a targeted partner to traditional harvests, they help cities conserve water, shorten supply chains, and keep nutritious produce accessible during extreme weather.

questions.explanation_zh: 第4段末句农业经济学家的观点非常平衡：垂直农场短期内不会取代乡村农田（will not replace rural farmland anytime soon），而是作为传统农业的有针对性补充（targeted partner）。
distractor_reasons: 正确：complement（补充）对应原文中的 targeted partner，准确反映“不替代、作补充”的定位。
错误：与原文 will not replace rural farmland anytime soon 直接相反。
错误：属于无中生有且曲解前景。
错误：文中强调供应本地超市和应对极端天气，而非专门出口奢华草莓。

reading_passages.title: Why Repair Cafes Are Drawing Young City Residents
reading_passages.title_zh: 城市维修咖啡馆为何吸引年轻居民

paragraphs.text: On the second Saturday of every month, a neighborhood community hall on Maple Street turns into a cheerful workshop filled with lamps, coffee kettles, and torn backpacks. Instead of dropping broken household items into curbside bins, young residents queue at folding tables where retired electricians and hobbyists inspect loose wires and jammed zippers free of charge. Visitors pay only for replacement parts when needed, and conversations flow easily over mugs of warm tea.

When the volunteer organizers launched this repair cafe two years ago, they expected mainly budget-conscious seniors to bring worn clocks or radios. To their surprise, university students and young engineers quickly became the most frequent participants. Many newcomers explained that modern sealed gadgets leave buyers feeling helpless once a warranty expires, so watching a simple fuse replacement restores a refreshing sense of practical control over everyday possessions.

Unlike commercial service counters that take devices behind closed doors, repair cafes invite owners to sit beside the volunteer and hold the flashlight. Guided hands-on involvement helps facilitate real skill transfer across generations, turning passive consumers into confident problem solvers. Organizers report that nearly two-thirds of items brought to the tables go home working again, which directly enhances neighborhood pride while sparing local landfills from avoidable electronic waste.

Local environmental officers note that fixing a handful of toasters will not single-handedly solve global manufacturing waste. Yet such gatherings contribute quietly to a broader cultural shift: neighbors begin borrowing tools instead of buying duplicates, and small schools have started weekend repair clubs. By making maintenance visible and social, community repair spaces deliver a lasting positive impact on both household budgets and urban sustainability. Even shy newcomers soon leave with new friends.

questions.stem: What surprised the organizers of the Maple Street repair cafe?
options: University students and young engineers turned out to be the main visitors.
Retired electricians charged high consultation fees per lamp.
Senior citizens refused to wait in line on Saturday mornings.
Almost no household items could be fixed without factory tools.
questions.answer: University students and young engineers turned out to be the main visitors.
questions.evidence_text: To their surprise, university students and young engineers quickly became the most frequent participants.

evidence_anchor.text_span: To their surprise, university students and young engineers quickly became the most frequent participants.

questions.explanation_zh: 第2段先写组织者原以为主要吸引注重预算的老年人，随后用 To their surprise 引出意外发现：大学生与年轻工程师迅速成为最常来的参与者。
distractor_reasons: 正确：main visitors 同义替换原文 most frequent participants。
错误：第1段明确说明检查修理免费（free of charge），只付零件费。
错误：文中未提老年人拒绝排队。
错误：第3段指出近三分之二物品被修好带回家。

questions.stem: How do repair cafes differ from commercial repair counters according to Paragraph 3?
options: Owners sit alongside volunteers and learn how the fix is done.
Commercial shops repair backpacks faster than community volunteers.
Repair cafes accept only unopened appliances still under warranty.
Volunteers take broken electronics home for private inspection.
questions.answer: Owners sit alongside volunteers and learn how the fix is done.
questions.evidence_text: Unlike commercial service counters that take devices behind closed doors, repair cafes invite owners to sit beside the volunteer and hold the flashlight.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Unlike commercial service counters that take devices behind closed doors, repair cafes invite owners to sit beside the volunteer and hold the flashlight.

questions.explanation_zh: 第3段对比商业维修柜台（把设备拿进后台）与维修咖啡馆：邀请物主坐在志愿者身旁一起参与并学习维修技能。
distractor_reasons: 正确：alongside volunteers 对应 beside the volunteer，概括了现场学技能的过程。
错误：文中未比较两者的修理速度。
错误：第2段明确是过了保修期的日常用品，并非未拆封保修期内电器。
错误：是当场在折叠桌旁共同检修，并非带回家。

questions.stem: Why do young buyers value watching a simple fuse replacement at the workshop?
options: It gives them back a sense of control over modern sealed products.
It guarantees that electronics companies will extend free warranties.
It lets them sell repaired appliances at higher prices online.
It replaces all formal engineering courses at local colleges.
questions.answer: It gives them back a sense of control over modern sealed products.
questions.evidence_text: Many newcomers explained that modern sealed gadgets leave buyers feeling helpless once a warranty expires, so watching a simple fuse replacement restores a refreshing sense of practical control over everyday possessions.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Many newcomers explained that modern sealed gadgets leave buyers feeling helpless once a warranty expires, so watching a simple fuse replacement restores a refreshing sense of practical control over everyday possessions.

questions.explanation_zh: 第2段末句说明：现代封闭式电子产品在过保后常让消费者感到无助，而亲眼看到更换保险丝这样的简单修理，能恢复对日常物品的掌控感。
distractor_reasons: 正确：直接对应 restores a refreshing sense of practical control。
错误：文中未提厂家延长保修。
错误：维修后带回自用，并未提及网上高价转卖。
错误：“取代所有大学工科课程”属于过度夸大。

questions.stem: What broader value do environmental officers see in repair cafes in Paragraph 4?
options: They encourage sharing habits and sustainable attitudes across neighborhoods.
They immediately eliminate the need for industrial waste regulations.
They persuade factories to stop producing small kitchen appliances.
They generate large profits for city hall every month.
questions.answer: They encourage sharing habits and sustainable attitudes across neighborhoods.
questions.evidence_text: Yet such gatherings contribute quietly to a broader cultural shift: neighbors begin borrowing tools instead of buying duplicates, and small schools have started weekend repair clubs.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Yet such gatherings contribute quietly to a broader cultural shift: neighbors begin borrowing tools instead of buying duplicates, and small schools have started weekend repair clubs.

questions.explanation_zh: 第4段先客观承认单靠修几台烤面包机无法彻底解决工业垃圾，随后用 Yet 指出其更深层文化价值：促进邻里共享工具与社区可持续习惯。
distractor_reasons: 正确：概括了邻里借用工具与可持续文化转变。
错误：首句明确说不会单凭此解决全球制造垃圾问题。
错误：无中生有。
错误：咖啡馆为公益志愿活动，并非市政府盈利项目。

reading_passages.title: How Micro-Breaks Protect Afternoon Office Focus
reading_passages.title_zh: 微休息如何保护午后工作专注力

paragraphs.text: Many office workers treat lunch as the only legitimate pause in an eight-hour workday, pushing through afternoon spreadsheets until their eyes ache. When mental focus inevitably fades around three o'clock, people often reach for extra coffee or force themselves to stare harder at the monitor. Yet occupational psychologists warn that skipping brief recovery moments quietly undermines both accuracy and overall productivity before closing time. Tired minds rarely notice subtle numerical errors during long editing sessions.

In a six-week study covering three hundred clerical employees, researchers tested the effect of taking three-minute micro-breaks every fifty minutes. Rather than checking social media feeds, participants stood up, stretched their shoulders, drank water, or looked out a window at distant trees. Even though these pauses subtracted nearly twenty minutes from desk time, the test group completed forms faster and made fewer typing errors. They also reported feeling noticeably calmer and more alert at five o'clock.

Scientists explain that how you spend those three minutes is a decisive factor in restoring energy. Scrolling through rapid news updates keeps the visual attention system locked on bright pixels, so mental fatigue barely diminishes. Stepping away from glowing screens to breathe calmly or chat briefly with a colleague gives working memory adequate space to reset, making it noticeably easier to concentrate upon returning to detailed analytical tasks and client messages.

Forward-thinking managers have therefore stopped equating constant chair time with genuine dedication. By encouraging teams to block short stretching windows between afternoon meetings, workplaces reduce burnout without lowering weekly output. Protecting small pockets of rest turns out to be a surprisingly practical investment in clearer thinking, steadier mood, and fewer late-day mistakes across busy corporate departments and customer teams.

questions.stem: What do many office workers typically do when afternoon focus drops around 3 p.m.?
options: They drink more coffee or keep staring harder at their screens.
They take a three-minute walk outdoors every fifty minutes.
They leave the office early to avoid making typing errors.
They ask managers to cancel all afternoon meetings.
questions.answer: They drink more coffee or keep staring harder at their screens.
questions.evidence_text: When mental focus inevitably fades around three o'clock, people often reach for extra coffee or force themselves to stare harder at the monitor.

evidence_anchor.text_span: When mental focus inevitably fades around three o'clock, people often reach for extra coffee or force themselves to stare harder at the monitor.

questions.explanation_zh: 第1段第2句直接交代三点钟注意力下滑时上班族的常见应对：多喝咖啡（reach for extra coffee）或硬逼自己盯着屏幕。
distractor_reasons: 正确：直接对应第1段第2句的常见做法。
错误：这是第2段实验组采用的新做法，并非大多数上班族平时的习惯。
错误：第1段说大家硬撑到下班，并非提前离开。
错误：文中未提要求取消所有下午会议。

questions.stem: What happened when employees took three-minute pauses every fifty minutes in the six-week study?
options: They worked faster and made fewer mistakes despite spending slightly less time at their desks.
Their daily form output fell sharply because twenty minutes were lost.
They spent the break time scrolling through social media feeds.
They needed extra coffee every afternoon to stay awake.
questions.answer: They worked faster and made fewer mistakes despite spending slightly less time at their desks.
questions.evidence_text: Even though these pauses subtracted nearly twenty minutes from desk time, the test group completed forms faster and made fewer typing errors.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Even though these pauses subtracted nearly twenty minutes from desk time, the test group completed forms faster and made fewer typing errors.

questions.explanation_zh: 第2段末句用 Even though 让步指出：虽然微休息扣除了近二十分钟工位时间，但实验组填表速度更快、打字错误更少。
distractor_reasons: 正确：accurately summarizes completed forms faster and made fewer typing errors。
错误：与原文“完成更快”相反。
错误：第2段明确说 Rather than checking social media feeds。
错误：文中未说实验组仍依赖额外咖啡。

questions.stem: Why does scrolling through phone news fail to refresh the mind during a short break?
options: It keeps visual attention fixed on bright screens instead of letting memory reset.
News articles are too boring to attract office workers' interest.
Reading updates forces workers to type long replies to colleagues.
Bright monitor light damages office keyboards over time.
questions.answer: It keeps visual attention fixed on bright screens instead of letting memory reset.
questions.evidence_text: Scrolling through rapid news updates keeps the visual attention system locked on bright pixels, so mental fatigue barely diminishes.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Scrolling through rapid news updates keeps the visual attention system locked on bright pixels, so mental fatigue barely diminishes.

questions.explanation_zh: 第3段解释道：刷快速新闻推送会让视觉注意力系统继续锁定在发光像素上（locked on bright pixels），精神疲劳几乎不会消退，而离开屏幕才能让工作记忆重置。
distractor_reasons: 正确：fixed on bright screens 同义替换 locked on bright pixels。
错误：无中生有。
错误：文中未提回复同事。
错误：无中生有。

questions.stem: What attitude do forward-thinking managers hold in Paragraph 4?
options: They value real mental recovery and steady output over nonstop sitting.
They forbid employees from talking with coworkers during work hours.
They want to shorten lunch breaks to fit in more stretching.
They believe late-day mistakes happen only when desks are messy.
questions.answer: They value real mental recovery and steady output over nonstop sitting.
questions.evidence_text: Forward-thinking managers have therefore stopped equating constant chair time with genuine dedication.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Forward-thinking managers have therefore stopped equating constant chair time with genuine dedication.

questions.explanation_zh: 第4段首句指出有远见的管理者不再把“一直坐在椅子上”等同于敬业，而是鼓励短暂拉伸休息，以在不降低周产出的前提下减少倦怠。
distractor_reasons: 正确：准确概括管理者重恢复与稳产出、不盲信死坐工位的态度。
错误：第3段提到与同事简短闲聊有益恢复，并非禁止交谈。
错误：文中未提缩短午休。
错误：与桌面整洁无关。

reading_passages.title: Designing Walkable University Campuses for Everyone
reading_passages.title_zh: 为所有人打造宜步行的友好大学校园

paragraphs.text: When visitors admire classic university campuses, they often praise stone archways and broad central lawns. Yet for students pushing heavy book carts, recovering from ankle sprains, or using wheelchairs, decorative staircases can quickly turn daily class transitions into frustrating obstacles. Modern campus architects therefore argue that visual beauty means little unless every lecture hall, dining center, and science laboratory remains effortlessly accessible to all students, staff, and visiting scholars.

Over the past decade, several engineering schools adopted a practical approach known as universal design. Instead of adding steep side ramps behind old buildings as an afterthought, planners build wide, gently sloped main entrances that welcome everyone through the same front doors. Automatic sliding glass panels and raised sidewalk crossings also enable delivery staff, parents with strollers, and hurried undergraduates to move smoothly between buildings even in crowded rush periods and rainy afternoons.

Research on campus movement shows that inclusive pathways prove broadly beneficial even for able-bodied pedestrians across large teaching zones. Shaded continuous walkways with clear directional signs encourage more students to walk instead of waiting for crowded shuttle buses between classes. Meanwhile, replacing uneven cobblestones with smooth, rain-draining pavement reduces minor slip accidents during wet autumn mornings and lowers long-term campus maintenance expenses across busy academic districts.

To keep improvements grounded in real student experience, two coastal universities now establish joint walkability panels before approving any renovation budget. Every semester, student volunteers walk evening routes alongside facilities engineers to spot dim streetlights, narrow doorways, and missing curb cuts. Listening to everyday walkers early prevents expensive redesigns later and helps campuses grow into genuinely welcoming communities. Thoughtful inclusive campus design serves students, weekend guests, visiting families, and older faculty members alike.

questions.stem: What problem do decorative campus staircases create according to Paragraph 1?
options: They make moving between classes difficult for injured students, wheelchair users, and cart pushers.
They block natural sunlight from reaching the central lawns.
They cost twice as much to clean as modern glass doors.
They force visitors to park outside the university gates.
questions.answer: They make moving between classes difficult for injured students, wheelchair users, and cart pushers.
questions.evidence_text: Yet for students pushing heavy book carts, recovering from ankle sprains, or using wheelchairs, decorative staircases can quickly turn daily class transitions into frustrating obstacles.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Yet for students pushing heavy book carts, recovering from ankle sprains, or using wheelchairs, decorative staircases can quickly turn daily class transitions into frustrating obstacles.

questions.explanation_zh: 第1段第2句明确指出：对于推沉重书车、脚踝扭伤康复中或坐轮椅的学生而言，装饰性楼梯会让日常课间穿行变成令人沮丧的障碍。
distractor_reasons: 正确：直接对应第1段中三类人群遇到的通行障碍。
错误：文中未提遮挡阳光。
错误：文中未比较清洁成本。
错误：未提及校外停车问题。

questions.stem: How does universal design handle building entrances in Paragraph 2?
options: It creates gently sloped main doors shared smoothly by everyone.
It hides narrow metal ramps behind old service alleys.
It bans delivery carts from entering academic halls.
It replaces all campus sidewalks with underground tunnels.
questions.answer: It creates gently sloped main doors shared smoothly by everyone.
questions.evidence_text: Instead of adding steep side ramps behind old buildings as an afterthought, planners build wide, gently sloped main entrances that welcome everyone through the same front doors.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Instead of adding steep side ramps behind old buildings as an afterthought, planners build wide, gently sloped main entrances that welcome everyone through the same front doors.

questions.explanation_zh: 第2段说明通用设计（universal design）的做法：不是事后在建筑背面补修陡峭侧坡，而是直接建设宽阔平缓的主入口，让所有人从同一扇前门顺畅进出。
distractor_reasons: 正确：精确概括 gently sloped main entrances that welcome everyone through the same front doors。
错误：这正是通用设计所摒弃的旧做法（Instead of adding steep side ramps behind old buildings）。
错误：第2段末句提到自动移门方便了送货人员（delivery staff）通行。
错误：文中未提地下通道。

questions.stem: What extra benefit comes from replacing uneven cobblestones with smooth draining pavement?
options: Fewer wet-morning slips and lower long-term repair costs.
Faster bicycle races through crowded central lawns.
Higher electricity output from campus streetlights.
More parking spaces for private cars near dormitories.
questions.answer: Fewer wet-morning slips and lower long-term repair costs.
questions.evidence_text: Meanwhile, replacing uneven cobblestones with smooth, rain-draining pavement reduces minor slip accidents during wet autumn mornings and lowers long-term campus maintenance expenses across busy academic districts.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Meanwhile, replacing uneven cobblestones with smooth, rain-draining pavement reduces minor slip accidents during wet autumn mornings and lowers long-term campus maintenance expenses across busy academic districts.

questions.explanation_zh: 第3段末句指出：将凹凸不平的鹅卵石路面换为平整透水路面，能减少潮湿秋晨的滑倒小事故，并降低长期维护费用（maintenance expenses 同义替换为 repair costs）。
distractor_reasons: 正确：直接对应 reduces minor slip accidents 与 lowers long-term campus maintenance expenses。
错误：文中未提自行车竞速。
错误：路灯发电属于无中生有。
错误：本段鼓励步行，并非增加私家车位。

questions.stem: Why do two coastal universities pair student volunteers with engineers on evening walks?
options: To catch real accessibility flaws early and avoid costly redesigns later.
To test whether students can memorize every campus building name.
To replace official building inspectors with unpaid undergraduates.
To decide which historic stone archways should be demolished.
questions.answer: To catch real accessibility flaws early and avoid costly redesigns later.
questions.evidence_text: Listening to everyday walkers early prevents expensive redesigns later and helps campuses grow into genuinely welcoming communities.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Listening to everyday walkers early prevents expensive redesigns later and helps campuses grow into genuinely welcoming communities.

questions.explanation_zh: 第4段说明两所沿海大学在批准翻修预算前组织学生志愿者与设施工程师夜走路线，旨在早发现昏暗路灯、窄门等问题，从而避免日后昂贵的返工重改（prevents expensive redesigns later）。
distractor_reasons: 正确：准确概括了早发现问题、避免高成本返工的目的。
错误：与背诵楼名无关。
错误：是与工程师共同巡查（alongside facilities engineers），并非取代正式检查员。
错误：文中未提拆除历史石拱门。

reading_passages.title: When AI Tutors Enter the Writing Classroom
reading_passages.title_zh: 当人工智能导师走进写作课堂

paragraphs.text: Over the past two semesters, several universities have introduced artificial intelligence writing assistants into introductory composition courses. Rather than banning automated tools outright, instructors wanted to test whether an adaptive digital tutor could help large classes receive timely feedback. In a traditional thirty-student section, learners often wait ten days for comments on an early draft, by which time their enthusiasm for revision has faded and the class has already moved to a new assignment.

Early classroom trials showed clear benefits on mechanical skills such as sentence variety, verb agreement, and paragraph transitions. When students received instant suggestions before submitting assignments, they corrected basic structural flaws on their own and arrived at office hours ready to discuss deeper ideas. Instructors also noticed that shy students, who rarely spoke during peer review workshops, felt more willing to test bold arguments privately with software before sharing them with classmates.

However, educators quickly spotted a troubling side effect when learners treated automated advice as an effortless shortcut. Some students accepted every proposed rewrite without questioning whether the polished wording still matched their original intent or evidence. As a result, essays began to sound remarkably similar, losing the personal voice and local examples that make freshman writing memorable and persuasive. Teachers worried that smooth phrasing was masking weak logic.

To preserve independent thinking, writing programs now pair digital tools with transparent process logs and oral check-ins. Students must annotate which software prompts they accepted, which suggestions they rejected, and why their final evidence supports the thesis. When learners actively evaluate machine feedback instead of copying it passively, AI serves as a tireless practice partner while human teachers focus on critical reasoning and mentoring.

reading_passages.title: Tiny City Forests Bring Cool Shade Back to Concrete Streets
reading_passages.title_zh: 城市微型森林为水泥街道带回清凉绿荫

paragraphs.text: In crowded neighborhoods where every square meter of land is prized for parking or housing, city planners rarely find space for sweeping parks. Lately, however, several municipalities have transformed neglected traffic islands and narrow schoolyards into dense micro-forests no larger than a tennis court. By planting dozens of native trees and shrubs closely together, these pocket woodlands create layered canopies that cool surrounding sidewalks during harsh summer heatwaves.

Unlike neatly spaced street trees surrounded by compacted pavement, micro-forests rely on rich soil prepared with compost and natural mulch before planting begins. Because young roots compete gently for sunlight and moisture in tight quarters, saplings grow upward much faster than isolated trees on open lawns. Within three years, a thriving plot can lower nearby surface temperatures by several degrees while offering welcome shade to waiting bus passengers and nearby pedestrians.

Beyond heat relief, these miniature ecosystems act as living sponges during heavy seasonal storms. Loose woodland soil absorbs sudden rainwater far more effectively than asphalt, reducing street flooding and easing pressure on aging underground drains. Local biology teachers also report that songbirds, butterflies, and helpful insects return within months, turning formerly barren concrete corners into lively outdoor classrooms for neighborhood children and curious residents.

Maintaining a micro-forest requires surprisingly little effort after its first two summers of regular watering and weeding. Once the leafy canopy closes overhead, weeds struggle to survive in the dim light beneath, and fallen leaves naturally recycle nutrients back into the earth. Urban ecologists note that while pocket forests cannot replace large regional reserves, multiplying small green patches across dense blocks offers a practical defense against rising city temperatures.

questions.stem: Where are cities typically planting micro-forests according to Paragraph 1?
options: Along distant mountain slopes outside city borders.
On neglected traffic islands and narrow schoolyards.

reading_passages.title: Digital Minimalism: Choosing Tools That Serve Your Time
reading_passages.title_zh: 数字极简主义：选择真正服务于你时间的工具

paragraphs.text: Most people assume that spending hours scrolling through feeds happens because they lack personal willpower. Yet behavioral designers point out that modern apps are built to capture human attention through endless updates, bright badges, and unpredictable rewards. Over time, checking a screen becomes an automatic reflex during every spare second in an elevator or checkout line, leaving users feeling curiously drained despite having done very little meaningful work.

In response, a growing movement called digital minimalism encourages people to rethink technology with clear purpose rather than rejecting it altogether. Advocates do not ask participants to abandon online banking, digital maps, or video calls with distant relatives. Instead, the core rule is to keep only tools that strongly support deeply held values while removing passive entertainment feeds that quietly steal evening hours from rest and study.

Practicing this shift usually begins with a thirty-day reset during which optional apps and social alerts are paused completely. Rather than staring at an empty desk, participants are urged to fill newly freed evenings with tangible offline activities such as cooking, repairing bicycles, or joining a local running club. Without a rewarding replacement routine, boredom quickly pushes most people back toward habitual scrolling late at night.

At the end of the trial month, people reintroduce only selected digital tools under strict boundaries, such as checking group messages once after dinner. Many university students who try the method report sharper focus during morning study blocks, steadier reading stamina, and calmer sleep before exams. Technology works best, minimalists argue, when it remains a deliberate servant rather than a noisy background habit that fragments every quiet hour and steals daily peace.

reading_passages.title: Morning Light and the Hidden Clock Inside Every Cell
reading_passages.title_zh: 晨光与每个细胞里的隐秘生物钟

paragraphs.text: Many college students blame late-night fatigue on weak coffee or heavy homework, yet sleep scientists point to a quieter cause: an out-of-sync internal clock. Known as the circadian rhythm, this roughly twenty-four-hour cycle governs not only when we feel drowsy or alert, but also body temperature, digestion, and hormone release. Nearly every tissue in the human body follows signals sent from a tiny master pacemaker deep inside the brain, coordinating daily energy peaks and restful recovery.

Among all daily cues, outdoor morning sunlight acts as the strongest reset button for that internal clock. Even on an overcast morning, stepping outside for fifteen minutes delivers far brighter light than standard classroom lamps. When natural light reaches specialized cells in the eye, it halts nighttime sleep hormones and schedules a steady rise in evening drowsiness roughly fourteen hours later, making bedtime feel effortless.

Trouble begins when modern schedules blur the contrast between day and night across busy campus weeks. Spending all morning behind drawn curtains and scrolling under bright blue screens after midnight confuses the brain into delaying its sleep signal. Students who sleep until noon on weekends experience what researchers call social jet lag, leaving Monday morning lectures feeling like an exhausting flight across three time zones.

Fortunately, restoring a steadier rhythm rarely demands harsh rules or expensive gadgets. Chronobiologists recommend three simple habits: getting natural daylight exposure soon after waking, keeping weekend wake times within an hour of weekday alarms, and dimming overhead lamps an hour before bed. When daily light and meal patterns grow predictable, daytime energy climbs naturally without relying on extra afternoon caffeine. Small, steady cues help every biological clock stay aligned across busy semesters.

questions.stem: Besides sleepiness, what else does the circadian rhythm regulate according to Paragraph 1?
options: Only the amount of coffee a student drinks at night.
Body temperature, digestion, and the release of hormones.

questions.evidence_text: Known as the circadian rhythm, this roughly twenty-four-hour cycle governs not only when we feel drowsy or alert, but also body temperature, digestion, and hormone release.

distractor_reasons: 错误：咖啡只是学生对疲劳的误归因对象，并非生物钟调控内容。

错误：文中未提及眼睛颜色。

reading_passages.title: Rethinking Teamwork Across Kitchen Tables and Time Zones
reading_passages.title_zh: 重新思考跨家庭书桌与时区的团队协作

paragraphs.text: When companies first shifted office teams to remote work, many managers simply moved an eight-hour office routine onto video calls. Within months, employees reported exhaustion from back-to-back camera meetings and constant chat pings that left little uninterrupted time for deep tasks. Ironically, teams felt both overly monitored throughout the workday and oddly disconnected from colleagues working only a few kilometers away in the very same city.

Organizational researchers soon discovered that successful virtual collaboration relies far more on written clarity than on constant online visibility. High-performing remote teams write down project goals, clear deadlines, and decision owners in shared documents that everyone can check across time zones. Instead of interrupting coworkers with quick status questions every hour, members leave structured daily updates and reserve live calls for complex problem-solving and creative brainstorming.

Still, pure efficiency cannot replace the informal trust that once grew naturally beside office coffee machines. New hires working from home often hesitate to ask small questions because typing into a public channel feels more intimidating than leaning over a desk. To bridge that gap, thoughtful managers pair newcomers with experienced teammates for brief weekly check-ins and host occasional in-person project kickoffs each quarter to strengthen personal bonds.

Equally vital is protecting personal boundaries when laptops sit inches away from family dinner tables. Companies that avoid late-night messaging and judge staff by completed results rather than green status dots report lower burnout and higher retention. Remote collaboration succeeds not by copying old office habits onto screens, but by designing intentional communication, mutual trust, and sustainable work rhythms. When expectations are written clearly and rest hours stay respected, distributed teams thrive over the long run.

questions.stem: What problem happened when managers copied traditional office routines onto video calls?
options: Employees finished all daily tasks in less than two hours.
Back-to-back meetings and chat pings exhausted staff and cut deep-work time.
Managers forgot to install cameras on company laptops.
Colleagues moved to different time zones without telling anyone.

reading_passages.title: Plastic-Eating Enzymes: Promise and Reality in Recycling
reading_passages.title_zh: 食塑酶：塑料回收中的希望与现实

paragraphs.text: In 2016, Japanese researchers examining soil outside a bottle recycling plant identified an unusual species of bacteria capable of feeding on PET, the durable plastic used in millions of beverage containers. The microbes produced specialized enzymes that snip long chemical chains back into basic building blocks. Headlines quickly celebrated the discovery as a miracle cure for overflowing landfills and polluted oceans worldwide. Yet laboratory curiosity rarely translates smoothly into city-scale waste infrastructure.

Chemists soon realized, however, that wild bacteria worked far too slowly for real-world waste management, taking weeks to break down a single thin film. By gently altering the enzyme's amino acid structure in the laboratory, engineering teams created faster variants able to digest shredded bottle flakes in heated tanks within hours. Unlike conventional melting, which weakens recycled fibers each time plastic is reused, biological recycling yields pure raw material ready for food-grade bottles and clear packaging.

Despite this technical leap, scaling enzyme recycling from gleaming lab reactors to industrial plants faces stubborn economic hurdles. Enzyme production requires sterile fermentation vats, precise temperature control, and chemical buffers that remain costly compared with cheap petroleum-based virgin plastic. Moreover, mixed household trash contains dyes, glues, and food grease that easily slow down delicate enzymes unless waste streams are carefully sorted and washed beforehand.

For these reasons, environmental engineers view plastic-eating enzymes as one valuable link in a broader circular strategy rather than an excuse to keep producing disposable packaging. Enzymatic plants may soon handle hard-to-recycle colored bottles and polyester textiles, while deposits, refill systems, and standardized packaging cut total waste upstream. Even the smartest biotechnology cannot outpace reckless consumption when single-use habits go unchecked.

questions.stem: What advantage does biological enzyme recycling have over conventional melting?
options: It converts plastic waste directly into cheap petroleum fuel.
It works at freezing temperatures inside ocean water.
It recovers pure base material without degrading fiber quality.
It eliminates the need to sort or wash household garbage.
questions.answer: It recovers pure base material without degrading fiber quality.
questions.evidence_text: Unlike conventional melting, which weakens recycled fibers each time plastic is reused, biological recycling yields pure raw material ready for food-grade bottles and clear packaging.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Unlike conventional melting, which weakens recycled fibers each time plastic is reused, biological recycling yields pure raw material ready for food-grade bottles and clear packaging.

reading_passages.title: Opening Every Gallery: How Museums Design for All Visitors
reading_passages.title_zh: 向所有人敞开大门：博物馆如何做全龄无障碍设计

paragraphs.text: For decades, public museums measured their success mainly by rare artifacts and grand marble staircases. Yet those impressive steps, dim lighting, and tiny printed labels quietly shut out elderly guests, wheelchair users, and visitors with low vision. Today, curators increasingly recognize that preserving human heritage means little if large parts of the community face physical or sensory barriers right at the front door of civic culture. Thoughtful design turns passive collections into welcoming shared spaces.

Modern accessibility begins well before a visitor steps into a gallery. Many institutions now publish detailed floor maps online showing elevator widths, quiet rest rooms, and loanable folding stools so guests can plan smoothly and feel confident upon arrival. Inside exhibition halls, designers pair traditional wall text with large-print booklets, tactile relief models of famous sculptures, and descriptive audio guides that explain brushwork, color, and composition in vivid everyday language.

Equally encouraging are low-sensory hours created for guests who find bright spotlights and echoing crowds overwhelming. Once a week, participating museums soften gallery lighting, lower hallway announcements, and invite families of children on the autism spectrum to explore exhibits at their own relaxed pace. Staff members receive practical training so they can assist politely without hovering nervously or making awkward assumptions.

Curators note a welcome surprise from these inclusive updates: features built for disability access end up helping nearly everyone who walks through the lobby. Parents pushing strollers rely on wide ramps, tired commuters appreciate extra benches, and foreign travelers follow clear visual icons and captioned videos effortlessly. When museums remove barriers for the margins, they make cultural life richer, warmer, and more welcoming for the entire public across generations.

reading_passages.title: The Quiet Drain of Forgotten Subscriptions
reading_passages.title_zh: 被遗忘的订阅：自动续费背后的静默开销

paragraphs.text: Whether signing up for cloud storage, language apps, or streaming music, modern consumers rarely buy digital tools once and own them outright. Instead, monthly automatic billing turns modest fees into effortless habits that silently renew in the background. When surveyed, most young adults underestimate their recurring digital spending by nearly half, shocked to discover unused plans still charging their student bank cards every single month.

Behavioral economists explain this gap through status quo bias and subtle friction in interface design. Signing up for a seven-day free trial takes two taps, yet ending the plan before charges begin often requires digging through nested account menus or calling customer service during narrow weekday hours. Facing small hassles, busy users postpone the task until next month, paying repeatedly for services they barely open on their phones.

Firms also rely on optimistic self-forecasting when pricing fitness memberships and online courses. People happily pay upfront for an annual bundle because they picture a disciplined future self exercising four times a week. Once midterms arrive and attendance drops, canceling feels like admitting personal failure, so consumers leave the automatic charge untouched in hopes of returning next Monday with fresh determination and spare energy.

Fortunately, simple rules and smarter tools are beginning to rebalance the scales for everyday buyers. Several consumer protection agencies now require companies to offer one-click online cancellation as easy as enrollment and to send clear renewal reminders before annual bills hit. Meanwhile, personal finance coaches suggest scheduling a ten-minute monthly audit of bank statements to keep small leaks from sinking a tight student budget over time. Checking recurring charges regularly turns mindless spending back into deliberate choice.

questions.stem: What do surveys reveal about young adults' awareness of their subscription costs?
options: They accurately track every monthly fee on paper spreadsheets.
They prefer paying large one-time prices rather than monthly fees.
They typically underestimate their recurring digital charges by almost fifty percent.
They cancel unused apps within forty-eight hours of free trials.
questions.answer: They typically underestimate their recurring digital charges by almost fifty percent.
questions.evidence_text: When surveyed, most young adults underestimate their recurring digital spending by nearly half, shocked to discover unused plans still charging their student bank cards every single month.

reading_passages.title: How Switching Between Languages Exercises the Brain
reading_passages.title_zh: 双语切换如何锻炼大脑执行功能

paragraphs.text: A century ago, some educators worried that raising children with two languages would confuse young minds and slow down school achievement. Modern brain imaging has thoroughly overturned that early assumption. Far from storing two languages in separate locked drawers, a bilingual brain keeps both vocabularies active at all times, even when a speaker is reading a novel or chatting quietly in only one language.

Because both languages compete quietly whenever a person reaches for a word, the brain must constantly select the right term while holding back the second system. Psychologists compare this silent mental traffic control to a skilled conductor directing two busy orchestras at once. Over years of daily practice, the constant filtering strengthens executive control, the set of skills used for planning, shifting attention, and ignoring unwanted distractions.

Interestingly, this mental workout carries visible trade-offs as well as clear cognitive benefits in laboratory settings. On timed picture-naming tests, bilingual adults occasionally pause a fraction of a second longer than monolingual peers because they manage a larger pool of words across two systems. Yet in tasks requiring rapid rule changes—such as sorting cards first by color and then suddenly by shape—bilingual participants often adapt faster with fewer errors.

Neuroscientists have also observed encouraging signs in aging populations across multiple cultural studies. While lifelong bilingualism does not prevent biological brain wear, studies across several countries suggest that habitual speakers of two languages often cope with memory decline noticeably longer before symptoms disrupt daily life. Learning a second language even in adulthood cannot guarantee immunity, yet every conversation gives neural networks fresh flexibility and lasting resilience in later decades.

options: Two languages are stored in completely separate, locked areas.
Speaking two languages permanently slows down reading speed.

questions.evidence_text: Far from storing two languages in separate locked drawers, a bilingual brain keeps both vocabularies active at all times, even when a speaker is reading a novel or chatting quietly in only one language.

reading_passages.title: Small Plates, Smart Menus: Cutting Campus Cafeteria Waste
reading_passages.title_zh: 小盘分餐与智能菜单：减少校园食堂食物浪费

paragraphs.text: At the end of every lunch rush, university dining halls face a troubling sight: bins overflowing with half-eaten rice, untouched vegetables, and discarded bread. While kitchen staff work hard to control cooking leftovers, surveys show that nearly sixty percent of campus food waste happens on student plates after meals are served. Hungry students often pile trays high with oversized portions before realizing their appetites are smaller than their eyes.

To tackle this habit without lecturing diners, several colleges tested a surprisingly simple nudge: removing plastic serving trays in self-serve cafeteria halls. When students must carry a plate and a cup in two hands, they naturally choose realistic portions on their first trip and return for seconds only if still hungry. Within one semester, trayless dining reduced post-meal plate waste by nearly a third while saving thousands of liters of dishwashing water.

Kitchen managers paired the tray change with flexible portion options and clearer menu signs. Instead of serving one giant scoop of rice by default, cooks now offer regular and half-sized servings at the counter. Meanwhile, electronic boards near the steam tables track popular dishes in real time, helping chefs cook smaller batches late in the evening so fewer unsold trays end up in the compost bin.

Student volunteers have also joined the effort by launching a campus alert app for surplus safe food. Whenever a faculty seminar or sports banquet ends with untouched boxed meals, organizers post the pickup location so nearby students can claim free dinner within twenty minutes. Together, smarter serving habits and quick sharing prove that cutting campus waste protects both tight budgets and the local environment.

reading_passages.title: More Than Quiet Shelves: How Neighborhood Libraries Rebuild Connection
reading_passages.title_zh: 不止于安静的书架：社区图书馆如何重建邻里联结

paragraphs.text: When e-books and fast online search engines became everyday tools, some observers predicted that small neighborhood libraries would soon turn into dusty museums. Yet visitor counts across many cities tell a very different story today. While fewer residents walk in solely to borrow printed encyclopedias, branch libraries remain among the few indoor public spaces where anyone can sit, study, or warm up without buying a cup of coffee.

To meet changing local needs, modern librarians have expanded what a library card unlocks beyond novels and newspapers. Many branches now run tool lending shelves stocked with sewing machines, garden shears, and air-quality meters that families rarely need to buy for once-a-year projects. Sharing durable equipment cuts household expenses while helping neighbors meet one another over practical weekend repairs and shared DIY hobbies. Even modest borrowing programs build lasting goodwill across busy residential blocks.

Libraries also serve as trusted bridges across generations and income groups in crowded urban districts. On weekday afternoons, retired engineers volunteer at homework tables alongside teenagers, while morning workshops help older residents spot online scams and navigate hospital booking apps. Unlike commercial workshops that charge steep enrollment fees, these neighborhood classes welcome newcomers openly and adjust smoothly to local questions.

Urban planners call such spaces vital civic infrastructure because social trust grows when strangers share reliable community resources week after week. Whether a student needs quiet Wi-Fi before exams or a parent seeks weekend story time, the local branch offers equal footing regardless of wallet size. Far from fading in the digital age, neighborhood libraries are proving more indispensable to daily civic life than ever before in modern cities.

questions.explanation_zh: 第3段末句对比指出，商业工作坊收取高昂报名费，而社区图书馆课程敞开大门接纳新居民，并根据当地问题灵活调整内容，由此可推断其消除了经济门槛并更贴合本地需求。

reading_passages.title: Local Microgrids Keep Neighborhood Lights On During Storms
reading_passages.title_zh: 本地微电网如何在风暴中守护社区灯火

paragraphs.text: For over a century, modern cities have relied on sprawling power grids that send electricity hundreds of kilometers from massive power plants to local neighborhoods. While that centralized model keeps costs low on calm days, one fallen transmission tower during a severe ice storm or summer heatwave can leave entire towns dark for days. As extreme weather grows more frequent, utilities are rethinking how communities generate and protect essential power.

One promising answer is the renewable microgrid, a localized energy network linking rooftop solar panels, community battery banks, and smart control software. During ordinary weeks, a microgrid connects smoothly to the main regional grid, sharing surplus clean electricity with nearby blocks. Yet the moment sensors detect a sudden outage on distant lines, automated switches isolate the neighborhood network within seconds so clinics, grocery stores, and traffic signals stay running stably.

Several university campuses and island towns have already proved the value of this flexible design. When coastal winds snapped regional cables last autumn, a community center powered by solar arrays and stored battery reserves kept refrigeration running for vital medicines and offered neighbors warm charging stations. Previously, those same buildings depended on noisy diesel generators whose fuel deliveries were easily blocked by flooded coastal roads.

To be sure, building microgrids requires substantial upfront investment in storage batteries and grid software, and engineers must balance local supply carefully during cloudy winter weeks. Still, falling battery prices and shared community ownership are making neighborhood resilience more affordable each year. Rather than replacing national grids, local microgrids act as sturdy safety nets that keep clean energy flowing reliably where people live and work.

questions.stem: What weakness of traditional centralized power grids is noted in Paragraph 1?
options: They produce more electricity than big cities can safely use.
They rely solely on rooftop solar panels that stop working at night.
Damage to one distant transmission line can black out whole towns for days.
They cost far more to operate during calm weather than storms.
questions.answer: Damage to one distant transmission line can black out whole towns for days.
questions.evidence_text: While that centralized model keeps costs low on calm days, one fallen transmission tower during a severe ice storm or summer heatwave can leave entire towns dark for days.

evidence_anchor.text_span: While that centralized model keeps costs low on calm days, one fallen transmission tower during a severe ice storm or summer heatwave can leave entire towns dark for days.

questions.explanation_zh: 第1段第2句指出，集中式大电网虽在风平浪静时成本较低，但暴风雪或热浪中只要倒塌一座输电塔，就可能让整座城镇停电数日。
distractor_reasons: 错误：文中未说发电量过剩危及安全。
错误：传统大电网依赖百公里外的大型电厂，而非屋顶光伏。
正确：直接对应一座输电塔故障导致整镇断电数日的脆弱性。
错误：原文明确说 keeps costs low on calm days。

questions.stem: What happens when a microgrid senses a sudden failure on distant regional lines?
options: It shuts down nearby clinics and traffic signals to save battery power.
It disconnects automatically within seconds to keep local essential services powered.
It sends emergency crews out to rebuild fallen transmission towers.
It switches off all solar panels until regional utilities restore service.
questions.answer: It disconnects automatically within seconds to keep local essential services powered.
questions.evidence_text: Yet the moment sensors detect a sudden outage on distant lines, automated switches isolate the neighborhood network within seconds so clinics, grocery stores, and traffic signals stay running stably.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Yet the moment sensors detect a sudden outage on distant lines, automated switches isolate the neighborhood network within seconds so clinics, grocery stores, and traffic signals stay running stably.

questions.explanation_zh: 第2段末句说明，一旦传感器检测到远方线路突发断电，自动开关会在几秒内将社区网络隔离运行（isolate the neighborhood network within seconds），保障诊所、杂货店和交通信号灯稳定运转。

questions.stem: Why were older diesel backup generators less reliable during severe coastal storms in Paragraph 3?
options: Diesel engines froze whenever temperatures rose in summer.
Island towns lacked skilled volunteers to turn on diesel switches.
Diesel generators produced too much quiet electricity for medical fridges.
Flooded roads could cut off the fuel deliveries needed to keep them running.
questions.answer: Flooded roads could cut off the fuel deliveries needed to keep them running.
questions.evidence_text: Previously, those same buildings depended on noisy diesel generators whose fuel deliveries were easily blocked by flooded coastal roads.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Previously, those same buildings depended on noisy diesel generators whose fuel deliveries were easily blocked by flooded coastal roads.

questions.explanation_zh: 第3段末句指出，以往那些建筑依赖吵闹的柴油发电机，而暴雨洪水淹没道路时，柴油燃料的运输补给很容易被阻断（fuel deliveries were easily blocked by flooded coastal roads）。

questions.stem: What challenges do engineers still face when expanding microgrids according to Paragraph 4?
options: High initial costs and managing power supply during cloudy winter weeks.
Strict bans on sharing clean electricity with neighboring blocks.
Lack of interest from university campuses and coastal communities.
Rising prices of community battery banks every single year.

questions.evidence_text: To be sure, building microgrids requires substantial upfront investment in storage batteries and grid software, and engineers must balance local supply carefully during cloudy winter weeks.

evidence_anchor.text_span: To be sure, building microgrids requires substantial upfront investment in storage batteries and grid software, and engineers must balance local supply carefully during cloudy winter weeks.

questions.explanation_zh: 第4段第1句指出两个现实挑战：储能电池和电网软件需要可观的前期投入（upfront investment），且工程师必须在阴云密布的冬季小心平衡本地供电。

questions.stem: How does the author view the relationship between local microgrids and national grids?
options: Microgrids will completely replace national power grids within a decade.
National grids should disconnect from all solar panels during ordinary weeks.
Microgrids serve as protective backups that complement national grids.
Microgrids are practical only for distant islands with no winter clouds.
questions.answer: Microgrids serve as protective backups that complement national grids.
questions.evidence_text: Rather than replacing national grids, local microgrids act as sturdy safety nets that keep clean energy flowing reliably where people live and work.

evidence_anchor.text_span: Rather than replacing national grids, local microgrids act as sturdy safety nets that keep clean energy flowing reliably where people live and work.

questions.explanation_zh: 第4段末句点明关系：本地微电网并非取代国家大电网，而是作为坚固的安全网（sturdy safety nets），与大电网互补并保障居民区的清洁电力供应。
